abstract: The expanding catalog of sQTLs from projects like GTEx has established that genetic risk for complex traits is frequently mediated through RNA splicing. Yet it is generally unknown whether disease-associated splice events produce stable, distinct protein isoforms and whether they are functionally consequent. Even the deepest shotgun proteomics efforts only capture a minority of annotated splice events; isoform-specific peptides are systematically under-sampled by nature of being lower abundance and intrinsically harder to detect. Here, we implement a genetics-guided targeted mass spectrometry (MS) strategy to detect splice-derived protein isoforms prioritized by sQTL colocalization. Using internal standard parallel reaction monitoring (IS-PRM), we targeted 288 peptides corresponding to 166 putative BMD-associated isoforms in differentiating osteoprogenitor cells and patient-derived primary mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). Targeted acquisition increased recovery of isoform-informative peptides relative to conventional DDA, rescued splice events that were undetected or sparsely sampled under global acquisition, and confirmed protein-level expression of genetically prioritized isoforms in clinical material. Together, this work establishes that targeted MS is a useful approach to support validation of protein expression in studies of the genetics of splicing.
